extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook guidance and description of how U.S. presidential nominations, campaigns, the Electoral College, inauguration, and early presidential powers and appointments operate in practice and by constitutional/statutory rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman of the national committee — campaign generalship
rubrics_metrics.description: The outcome of the campaign depends in a great measure upon the generalship of the chairman of the national committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairman 'surveys the whole field with the eye of an experienced general, discovering weak places, hurrying up reenforcements to doubtful states' and allocates resources strategically to win pivotal contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treasurer of the national committee — fundraising role
rubrics_metrics.description: The treasurer's business is to discover innumerable ways of raising the million dollars or more required to wage the great political contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treasurer should be a financier influential in wealthy circles; fundraising can leverage campaign issues to appeal to business interests (example: Wanamaker's appeals to businessmen about 'insurance' against bad economic years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign headquarters location as a strategic choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategic value of putting the centre of the campaign near or in the doubtful states is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may choose a single centre or divide headquarters into branches (examples: Republicans used Chicago in 1896; in 1900 they had New York and Chicago).

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign literature — required contents and targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Each party publishes a campaign text-book containing the platform, notification and acceptance speeches, biographical sketches, statistics on economic issues, addresses by leaders, and cogent arguments in support of the party's position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text-books are sent especially to newspapers and speakers (not the public broadly); supplemented by congressional committee text-books and innumerable pamphlets, leaflets, posters, cartoons, and speeches printed in all languages represented by voters; a bureau of printing directs production and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of newspapers to reach the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are a far more effective way of reaching the public than sending many printed packages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National committees use everything from great city dailies to rural weeklies to reach readers; overreliance on mass mailing can be wasteful while newspapers reach regular readers more directly (example: 1896 Republican committee estimated to reach five million families weekly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureau of public speakers — organization and deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: National committees generally have a bureau of public speakers which prepares a list of available orators by testing applicants and drafting volunteers, and directs the speakers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers range from street-corner haranguers to finished orators; headquarters lays out itineraries, engages halls and bands, organizes parades, and places speakers where their talents are most effective (estimates: thousands of local volunteers and many speeches daily in campaign peaks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate campaigning strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates either travel extensively delivering hundreds of speeches or remain at home and address crowds brought in by excursions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include Bryan's 400 reported speeches in 29 states (1896), McKinley's effective home campaigning in Canton, Taft's mileage and hundreds of speeches in 1908; choice of strategy depends on candidate and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political census and canvassing of doubtful states
rubrics_metrics.description: Early in the campaign a political census is taken of states known to vacillate; reliable and efficient canvassers are selected and paid to make a complete and accurate census.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party thereby gains an accurate count of votes it can rely on and a list of doubtful persons to influence; results are used like a military staff to dispatch targeted means of persuasion (example: detailed Iowa canvass in 1896 costing over $200,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for appointing electors
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors of each state are to be chosen as the legislature thereof may determine; historically three methods have been used: (1) legislative appointment, (2) popular election with some electors at large and some by congressional district, (3) popular election by general ticket statewide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice moved from legislative appointment to popular methods and ultimately to general ticket statewide elections to concentrate a state's influence by carrying all electors for one party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility restriction for electors
rubrics_metrics.description: No Senator or Representative or person holding any office of trust under the United States shall be appointed an elector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision removes electors from direct contact with the federal government and attempts separation between federal officials and the Electoral College.

rubrics_metrics.name: How voters cast ballots for President/Vice-President
rubrics_metrics.description: On election day the voter does not vote directly for President and Vice-President; if he votes a straight ticket he votes for the entire list of electors put forward by his party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Splitting the vote for presidential electors has no point unless there is a fusion arrangement; party lists appear on ballots for voter information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winner-take-all effect of state plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally the party which secures a plurality of votes in any state is entitled to all of the electoral votes of that state for President and Vice-President, no matter how large the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This system can produce Presidents elected by a minority of the national popular vote; it concentrates campaigns in 'close' states, incentivizes aggressive tactics there (including questionable uses of money), and reduces incentives to pile up votes in safe states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors' meeting, voting, certification, and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal law provides that electors of each commonwealth shall convene on the second Monday of January at such place as the state legislature may direct; they vote by ballot for President and Vice-President, make distinct lists of votes, sign, certify, seal, and transmit the lists to the president of the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least one of the two persons voted for must not be an inhabitant of the same state with the electors; certificates of election are evidence of their power to act and are crucial in contested elections; electors are treated as state officers and look to states for remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting of the electoral vote in Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The counting of the total electoral vote begins in the Hall of the House of Representatives on the second Wednesday of February with the president of the Senate in the chair; two tellers appointed by each chamber open and read the certificates in alphabetical state order and list the votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except in contested elections, the count is a formality since the result is ordinarily known months earlier; procedures for disputed returns have been created by Congress (reference to 1876 crisis and subsequent act).

rubrics_metrics.name: House election of President when no electoral majority
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate receives a majority of all the electoral votes, the House of Representatives chooses the President by ballot from the three candidates who have received the highest number of votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each state delegation in the House has one vote; a quorum consists of members from two-thirds of the states; a majority of all the states is necessary to choice; if the House fails to choose before March 4, the Vice-President acts as President. Historical instances: Jefferson (1801) and J.Q. Adams (1825).

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate election of Vice-President when no electoral majority
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever no candidate for Vice-President receives a majority of all the electoral votes, the election is thrown into the Senate, and the Senators, voting as individuals, choose the Vice-President from the two candidates having the highest number of votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-thirds of the whole number of Senators constitute a quorum for this purpose, and a majority of the whole number is necessary to a choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional qualifications for President and Vice-President
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be a natural-born citizen, at least thirty-five years old, and must have been fourteen years a resident within the United States; the same qualifications apply to the Vice-President; the term is four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So far as the Constitution is concerned, the President or Vice-President may be reelected indefinitely; political practice has added norms (see two-term tradition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-term political tradition (third-term doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political practice added a third requirement: no person is eligible to the office of President for more than two terms, at least in succession — the 'third term doctrine'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine rests on Washington's example rather than constitutional text; it became a strong political norm though not legally binding; it has been debated in cases such as Roosevelt 1912.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory line of succession beyond Vice-President (1886)
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of the death or resignation of both the President and Vice-President the following officers shall serve in the order mentioned: Secretary of State, of the Treasury, of War, the Attorney-General, the Postmaster-General, the Secretary of the Navy, and of the Interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory order (provided by Congress in 1886) governs succession beyond the Vice-President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inauguration formalities and oath administration
rubrics_metrics.description: No official notice is given to the President-elect; on the fourth of March he appears to take the oath of office, usually administered by the Chief Justice in the open air upon the platform built at the east front of the Capitol; if weather prevents the oath is taken in the Senate chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President-elect typically arrives days before, calls on the retiring President, is conducted to the Capitol by a committee on ceremonies, delivers an inaugural address, and views a long procession from a reviewing-stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet selection practice and confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: After installation the President selects his Cabinet and fills many minor places; he usually confines appointments to members of his own party but sometimes appoints opposition members; he attempts geographic balance and selects men he can work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabinet nominations must be confirmed by the Senate; as a matter of practice the Senate generally accepts the President's selections, making the Cabinet in practice his personal retinue for cooperation and advice; appointments sometimes reward prominent campaign supporters (examples: Wanamaker, Hitchcock).

rubrics_metrics.name: President's duty to enforce laws and direction of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the President's duty to see that the Constitution, laws, and treaties of the United States, and judicial decisions rendered by the federal courts are duly enforced everywhere throughout the United States; he may direct department heads and subordinates in discharge of their functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exact degree to which he may control administrative officers is politically controversial and depends on personality and constitutional theory; some departments (e.g., State in foreign affairs) are more directly subject to the President; the President can remove heads who refuse to obey and has ordinance power to supplement statutes by rules and regulations (historical example: Jackson's removal of Treasury secretaries).
